title: Compact client surface: seekable streaming, idempotent fetch & retry compatibility PRD
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Goal: Define a compact, language-agnostic client surface and server contract that enables: (1) low-latency streaming responses with seekable/resumable semantics, (2) idempotent and partial retries for long-running streams and paged fetches, and (3) clear compatibility guarantees across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs.

Scope: This PRD covers API shapes, wire-level markers (sequence numbers / cursors), retry semantics, backoff guidance, compatibility policy for minor/major changes, diagnostics/metrics, and acceptance criteria. Implementation and SDK ergonomics will be split into subsequent engineering tasks per language.

Out of scope: full SDK idiomatic wrappers (detailed language-specific ergonomic sugar), transport-layer pluggable adapters (left to later RFC), and offline/air-gapped packaging for private deployments (will follow security review).

Background/context: Teams building live assistants and document iterators need predictable ways to resume partial streams (e.g., after a client disconnect) and to retry failed chunks without replaying entire tokens. Current streaming primitives vary across languages and SDKs; we need a single server-side contract (sequence-id + checkpoint cursor) and a recommended client surface that maps cleanly to Python async iterators, TS AsyncIterator / ReadableStream, and Go channels/context patterns.

User stories:
- As an app engineer, I want to resume a text generation stream from the last-acknowledged token so users don't lose partial output after transient network blips.
- As a backend engineer, I want idempotent fetch endpoints for paged results so retries do not return duplicate records or inconsistent ordering.
- As an SDK maintainer, I want a compatibility matrix and deprecation timeline so we can safely roll out contract changes with minimal client churn.

Key requirements (high level):
1) Server stream framing: every stream chunk must include a strictly increasing sequence_id (64-bit int or string) and an optional checkpoint cursor (opaque string) representing the minimal resume point.
2) Checkpoint semantics: cursors are opaque tokens mapping to server-side prefix/KV cache entries; they are valid for a configurable TTL (default 24h) and must be stable for the expiry window.
3) Resume handshake: client can open a stream with resume_cursor to receive any missing chunks starting after the cursor. Server must validate cursor and either resume or return an explicit error code (INVALID_CURSOR / EXPIRED_CURSOR).
4) Partial-idempotent retries: for paged fetches and append-only streams, clients may provide an idempotency_key to allow server-side deduplication of side-effects and safe retry semantics.
5) Pagination contract: support both cursor-based and offset-style pagination on list endpoints. Cursor-based endpoints must return next_cursor when more results available and total_count only when inexpensive; offset endpoints remain supported for compatibility but discouraged for large result sets.
6) Backpressure & flow control: streaming endpoints must support client-specified max_in_flight_token_estimate and server-side throttling with explicit WAIT frames so clients can adapt batching.
7) Error model & retry guidance: define canonical error classes (TRANSIENT, PERMANENT, RATE_LIMIT, AUTH, INVALID_CURSOR) with suggested retry/backoff strategies; recommend exponential backoff with jitter for TRANSIENT and fixed behavior for RATE_LIMIT (respect Retry-After).
8) Compatibility guarantees: minor server-side improvements (perf, additional optional fields) are allowed without breaking clients for the next 12 months; any renaming of required fields is a major change and requires explicit deprecation window and migration docs.
9) Observability: streams must emit per-stream metrics: bytes_sent, tokens_sent, resume_attempts, successful_resumes, failed_resumes, avg_latency_ms, and last_seq_id. SDKs should surface these as counters/gauges to the console.

Acceptance criteria (each item must be demonstrable in staging):
acceptance_criteria: Streaming chunks include sequence_id and optional resume_cursor in RFC-structured JSON frames for all streamable endpoints.
Clients can successfully resume a streaming session from a previously recorded resume_cursor within the TTL in 95% of simulated network-recovery scenarios in the canary test harness.
Paged list endpoints support cursor-based pagination and return next_cursor when appropriate; at least one endpoint demonstrates cursor TTL enforcement and expiry error handling.

SDK prototypes (Python async iterator, TS AsyncIterator + ReadableStream, Go channel-based wrapper) implement resume handshake and idempotency_key propagation and pass end-to-end tests against staging server.
Retry guidance documented with machine-readable policy examples and unit tests exercising exponential backoff with jitter and handling of RATE_LIMIT Retry-After.
Compatibility policy (minor vs major change matrix + 12-month minor stability guarantee) published in SDK repo README and referenced from server changelog.
Metrics emitted by server and surfaced in Redwood Console per stream; dashboards demonstrate resumed vs non-resumed traffic, and alert rule created for repeated resume failures (>1% over 5m).
Security review sign-off obtained for resume cursor encoding/validation and idempotency behavior for customers on Private deployments.
decisions: Use opaque resume_cursor tokens instead of exposing internal offsets to allow server-side flexibility in compaction and caching strategies.
Include a sequence_id for every chunk to simplify ordering checks and to support partial replay semantics on clients.
Support both cursor-based and offset pagination during migration; recommend cursor-based for new endpoints and mark offset endpoints for eventual deprecation with a 9-12 month window.
Expose retry error classes via a short machine-readable field (error_class) and human-readable message to aid SDK surface mapping.
Default resume_cursor TTL set to 24h for hosted, configurable for Dedicated/Private customers via tenant config.
tradeoffs: Opaque cursors simplify server-side changes but require careful TTL and storage management; increases server-side state overhead compared to stateless offsets.
Adding sequence_id to every chunk increases payload slightly; tradeoff accepted to enable robust reorder detection and resumability.
Supporting both cursor and offset pagination increases API surface and docs burden; chosen to ease migration for existing customers while steering new users toward cursor-based flows.
